fr:mainmatter.html:p: A precise, self-contained account of three things the derivative-parser plan keeps circling, and how they fit together: (1) what the derivative parser is (sss-00F2), (2) what an automaton is here (sss-00F3), and (3) how to implement automaton parsers by Löb induction (sss-00F4). The emphasis is on getting the variances right — the tempting slogan "automata are coalgebras, parsers are algebras, glued by \mu =\nu " is imprecise, and the corrections are the point.

Calculus. Everything is internal to the dependent Lambek calculus: grammars are its linear types, A \vdash B is entailment, and \otimes , \multimap , \oplus , \mathrel {\And }, I, \top , \bot are the internal type formers. It is the linear residual of sss-00A7 (there written A ⟜ char c), an internal grammar — a linear hom — so the automaton transition is an operation of the calculus, not a map on an external state set. See also the syntactic derivative.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The derivative parser is the run

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fix the internal answer grammar \mathrm {Ans}_G := G \oplus \neg G (decide-and-produce; the parse forest is the left injection). It carries two free, internal properties (setup in sss-00F1):

html:ul.html:li: nullability \nu ?\,G, a decision of \nu G: the map that at \varepsilon picks an inhabitant of \mathrm {Ans}_G. Finite and structural on the guarded fragment.
derivative commutes \delta _c \mathrm {Ans}_G \;\cong \; \mathrm {Ans}_{\delta _c G}, since \delta _c is a right adjoint (preserves \oplus ) and commutes with \neg . Definitional.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The derivative parser of G is the entailment

read off the guarded first-character decomposition \top \;\cong \; I \;\oplus \; \bigoplus _c \lceil {c}\rceil \otimes \rhd \top : at the I summand answer \nu ?\,G; at the \lceil {c}\rceil \otimes \rhd \top summand consume c and, later, run \mathsf {parse}_{\delta _c G}, transporting the result along \delta _c \mathrm {Ans}_G \cong \mathrm {Ans}_{\delta _c G}. So the parser walks the input, replacing G by \delta _c G at each character, and answers with \nu ? at the end — the automaton run, closed by Löb.

Why it is a run, not a single-carrier fold. Unfolding a \Phi -algebra on a grammar A, for \Phi X = I \oplus \bigoplus _c \lceil {c}\rceil \otimes X (via the coproduct and \lceil {c}\rceil \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}}\dashv \delta _c), yields a base I \vdash A plus prepend maps A \vdash \delta _c A. The run instead transports the answer the other way, \delta _c\mathrm {Ans}_G \cong \mathrm {Ans}_{\delta _c G}, moving the grammar G \rightsquigarrow \delta _c G under the guard. So it is not a catamorphism into a fixed carrier; it is the guarded unfolding of sss-00F4.

Existence and uniqueness are Löb's, internal to the calculus: the recursive occurrence sits under \rhd , so \mathsf {parse}_G is the unique entailment satisfying the two clauses above. Uniqueness is the correctness statement — the c2a / family-hylomorphism reading of sss-00A9/sss-00F0.

fr:title.text: Sketch: the CFG derivative parser internal to LambekD

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sketch: the CFG derivative parser internal to LambekD

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Feasibility sketch for building the inductive derivative parser inside Lambek^{D} in Agda. The claim: it is definable and provable by combining the regex \delta + soundness on the brzozowski branch with \rhd /lob on the box branch; the one design decision is to put the guard in the datatype, and the one genuine risk is refl-time computation. Signatures below are schematic — proofs are holes, never postulates.

fr:title.text: Datatype: guard as a structural invariant

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Datatype: guard as a structural invariant

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The naive recursion δ c (var X) = δ c (def X) does not pass Agda's termination checker — def X is not a subterm and the keystone short-circuit is semantic. So encode the guard structurally, Greibach-style: a nonterminal is its finite list of guarded clauses ⌈c⌉ ⊗ tail.

NT : Type -- finite context of nonterminals (e.g. Fin n)
data CFGDesc : Type where ⟨I⟩ ⟨⊥⟩ : CFGDesc -- ε , empty lit : ⟨ Alphabet ⟩ → CFGDesc -- ⌈c⌉ var : NT → CFGDesc -- nonterminal leaf _⊗_ _⊕_ : CFGDesc → CFGDesc → CFGDesc
record Production : Type where -- one nonterminal's productions field nullable : Bool -- is ε accepted? clauses : List (Alphabet × CFGDesc) -- guarded: (leading char , tail)
def : NT → Production -- the grammar = a table of productions
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The invariant "every var occurs behind a consumed terminal" is now unforgeable: a nonterminal reaches you only via a clauses entry, whose head is a literal. Unguarded grammars are not expressible.

fr:title.text: Syntactic derivatives as an inductive CFG→CFG operation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Syntactic derivatives as an inductive CFG→CFG operation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: To parse without solving for the reachable states yourself, present grammars as a syntax and define \delta _c once, structurally, as a map on that syntax — a total CFGDesc → CFGDesc operation. This spells out the inductive construction sketched in sss-00A6: what the datatype is, why \delta _c is total on it, and why the recursion case does not diverge. It is the concrete bridge from CFGDesc to the generic Löb parser.

fr:title.text: The datatype

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fix a finite context \Gamma of nonterminals. A CFGDesc Γ is built from

html:ul.html:li: var X for X \in \Gamma — a nonterminal leaf;
I (the \varepsilon grammar), ⊥ (empty), ⌈c⌉ (a literal);
A ⊗ B (concatenation) and A ⊕ B (alternation).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A grammar equips each X \in \Gamma with a production def X : CFGDesc Γ, subject to the guard: in every def X, each var Y occurs under some ⌈c⌉ ⊗ (−) (no nonterminal is reachable without first consuming a terminal). This is the \rhd -guard at the level of descriptions. Dyck is def D = I ⊕ ⌈a⌉ ⊗ var D ⊗ ⌈b⌉ ⊗ var D.

fr:title.text: Nullability, inductively

fr:mainmatter.html:p: ν? : CFGDesc Γ → Bool is structural:

html:ul.html:li: ν? ⊥ = false, ν? I = true, ν? ⌈c⌉ = false;
ν? (A ⊕ B) = ν? A ∨ ν? B;
ν? (A ⊗ B) = ν? A ∧ ν? B;
ν? (var X) = ν? (def X).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The last clause looks circular but is not, because of the guard: inside def X every var Y sits under a ⌈c⌉ ⊗ (−), and ν? (⌈c⌉ ⊗ −) = false ∧ − = false short-circuits before any ν? (var Y) is consulted. So a nonterminal's nullability depends only on its terminal-free (base) clauses — a finite, non-recursive table. This is the "nullability collapses" half of the keystone.

fr:title.text: The derivative, inductively

fr:mainmatter.html:p: δ c : CFGDesc Γ → CFGDesc Γ — note the same \Gamma : the residual carries the original nonterminals as leaves. On the description formers it is the classical Brzozowski recursion:

html:ul.html:li: δ c ⊥ = ⊥, δ c I = ⊥;
δ c ⌈c'⌉ = I if c' = c, else ⊥;
δ c (A ⊕ B) = δ c A ⊕ δ c B;
δ c (A ⊗ B) = δ c A ⊗ B ⊕ (if ν? A then δ c B else ⊥).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The \otimes -clause is the whole game, and it must short- circuit: when ν? A = false, the second summand is ⊥ and δ c B is not computed. The nonterminal case unfolds once:

html:ul.html:li: δ c (var X) = δ c (def X).

fr:title.text: Why this terminates and stays a CFG

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why this terminates and stays a CFG

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Totality / structurality. The only non-structural clause is δ c (var X) = δ c (def X), and it fires at most once per nonterminal per step: differentiating def X, every var Y it contains sits behind a guard ⌈c'⌉ ⊗ (−), so the \otimes -clause short-circuits (ν? ⌈c'⌉ = false) and δ c (var Y) is never reached. Hence no nested δ c (var −) call, no divergence — one unfold and a finite structural pass. This is exactly the keystone lemma: the guard keeps the self-differentiation gate shut, so δ is total by structural recursion with no auxiliary fixed point.

Closure. δ c G is again a CFGDesc Γ over the same nonterminals — the residual mentions var X, never a differentiated nonterminal. So CFGDesc Γ is closed under δ, and iterating \delta stays in the syntax. The description grows (the \otimes - clause copies B), which is the unbounded state space showing up as unbounded term size; keeping it small is compaction — generic \bot /I-unit rewrites, an optimization, decoupled from totality.

Dyck check. δ a (var D) = δ a (def D) = δ a I ⊕ δ a (⌈a⌉ ⊗ (D ⊗ ⌈b⌉ ⊗ D)). The literal clause gives I ⊗ (D ⊗ ⌈b⌉ ⊗ D); the tail branch ν? ⌈a⌉ · δ a (…) short-circuits to ⊥ (never touching δ a (var D)). Result: D ⊗ ⌈b⌉ ⊗ D. Symmetrically δ b (var D) = ⊥. The stack states are whatever these iterates produce — the construction never names them.

fr:title.text: Parsing with derivatives for a locally contractive family of grammars

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parsing with derivatives for a locally contractive family of grammars

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Goal. Give a single, generic parser — producing parse trees, not an accept/reject bit — that works for any locally contractive endofunctor F on families of grammars, taking local-contractivity of F as the only hypothesis. In the intrinsic setting a grammar is its family of parse trees: a parse of w in G is an element of ⟦G⟧ w. So the parser must produce inhabitants of ⟦G*⟧ w (a whole forest, for ambiguous G), and the derivative must carry those inhabitants. This is the confluence of the derivative cluster with the local-contractivity / hylomorphism machinery: a recursive grammar family is the unique fixed point of a locally contractive functor, and its parser is the family hylomorphism that transports parse trees through the chain of derivative isomorphisms.

Conventions as in sss-00EZ, but read proof-relevantly: ε is the empty-string grammar, ⊥ the empty grammar, · concatenation, ⊕ alternation, char a a literal, δ c the derivative. Write ν G for the ε-part grammar of G — the subgrammar carrying exactly G's empty-string parses, (ν G) ε = G ε and ⊥ elsewhere. This is a grammar (it holds parse trees), not a Boolean; the recognizer's ν? is only its collapse to inhabited-or-not.

fr:title.text: Setup: a family of grammars as the fixed point of a contractive functor

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Setup: a family of grammars as the fixed point of a contractive functor

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Grammars are presheaves over (\stringg , \sqsubseteq ), \sqsubseteq the suffix order. A family of grammars is G : I \to \mathbf {Gr} for an index type I (the nonterminals / reachable derivative states). The later modality \rhd is front-consuming, (\rhd G)\,w = \prod _{u \sqsubset w} G\,u.

A functor F : \mathbf {Gr}^I \to \mathbf {Gr}^I is locally contractive when it factors through \rhd fibrewise — F(G)_i\,w depends on G only at proper suffixes of w. By the combinator calculus this is automatic when F is built from constants, the one-step guards char a · (−), and ⊕ / · / ⊗ positionwise: the grammar functor language, i.e. the string-ranked containers. Local contractivity gives a unique fixed point G^\ast = \mu F \cong F(G^\ast ) (Löb / Banach) — the recursive grammar family we parse. "F locally contractive" replaces every earlier guardedness device.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Step 1 — the derivative is a proof-relevant iso; parsing transports trees

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every grammar decomposes by first character, as a grammar isomorphism that carries parse trees:
G ≅ ν G ⊕ ⊕[c] char c · δ c G.
A parse of ε lands in ν G; a parse of c ∷ w splits as "the character c, then a parse of δ c G on w". The engine of the whole construction is the derivative iso
deriv : char c · G ≅ δ c G , equivalently (δ c G) w ≅ G (c ∷ w) ,
which is proof-relevant both ways: deriv pushes a "c-then-G" tree into a δ c G tree, and deriv⁻¹ recovers it. This is the ⟜-as-derivative content, not a decision.

The guard behaves as the character-indexed \rhd _c of sss-00AC, and the derivative is its force: from the adjunction {\mathopen {}\left (\char c \cdot -\right )\mathclose {}} \dashv \delta c of sss-00EY,

html:p.html:code: δ c (char c · G) = δ c(char c) · G ⊕ ν(char c) · δ c G = ε · G ⊕ ⊥ = G

fr:title.text: Step 2 — functor-level keystone: local contractivity makes δ total

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Step 2 — functor-level keystone: local contractivity makes δ total

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Lemma. If F is locally contractive then, for every family G, δ c (F G) depends on G but not on δ c G.

Proof. Push δ c through F by the (proof-relevant) chain rule δ c (A · B) = δ c A · B ⊕ ν A · δ c B. Every recursive occurrence of G sits under a guard char a · (⋯G⋯) — that is what local contractivity is. The branch that would recurse toward δ c G is ν(char a) · δ c(⋯G⋯), and ν(char a) = ⊥ (a literal has no empty parse) kills it; the other branch keeps (⋯G⋯), hence G, undifferentiated. So δ c(F G) never contains δ c G. ∎

Consequence. On the fixed point δ c G^\ast = δ c(F G^\ast ) is a residual over G^\ast (undifferentiated) and derivatives of the non-recursive parts — computed by one unfolding of F, no circular δ c G^\ast . Hence δ c is total on the whole reachable derivative family, generically, for any locally contractive F. This promotes the sss-00EZ keystone from a syntactic argument to a corollary of local contractivity — and because δ is proof-relevant, it transports parse trees while it goes.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Step 3 — the parser as a family hylomorphism

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The parser produces the parse forest parse G* w : ⟦G*⟧ w by walking the derivative isos down to ε and reshaping back:

html:p.html:code: parse G* ε = the ε-parses of G* ( inhabitants of (ν G*) ε )
parse G* (c ∷ w) = deriv⁻¹ (parse (δ c G*) w)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: where parse (δ c G*) w : (δ c G*) w reshapes along (δ c G*) w ≅ G* (c ∷ w) into a parse of the full string. Nothing here is Boolean: each step transports an actual tree, and the ε-base returns the set of empty-string parse trees (many, for ambiguous G*), so the output is the full parse forest.

This is exactly a HyloFam: the coalgebra unfolds the input against the derivative dynamics δ (the contractive strength, sss-00EP/sss-00EO; the mate G\circ H\circ U is locally contractive), and the algebra folds parse trees back up through deriv⁻¹; the carrier is the parse family ⟦G*⟧. Totality combines (i) each δ c step total (Step 2) with (ii) structural recursion on the input, terminating in |w| steps. The reachable derivative family is infinite for non-regular G^\ast , but a single parse visits only the length-|w| path — the hylo never materialises the state space.

html:p.html:code: parse G (c ∷ w) = deriv⁻¹ (parse (δ c G) w)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Here ν? below is only the nullability gate inside δ's definition (does the empty-string part exist), not the output.
The derivative is computed by pushing δ c through the grammar structure. The two rules that recurse into subgrammars are the ones to watch:

html:p.html:code: δ c (A ⊕ B) = δ c A ⊕ δ c B
δ c (A · B) = δ c A · B ⊕ ν? A · δ c B

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The product rule is the subtle one. Differentiating a concatenation A · B has two cases: either the first character came from A (giving δ c A · B), or A could match the empty string and the first character came from B (giving δ c B, but only if A is nullable — hence the ν? A gate).
Where general CFGs break. For a recursive grammar the derivative can refer back to itself. Take the left-recursive E = (E · char a) ⊕ char b. Differentiating:

html:p.html:code: δ a E = δ a (E · char a) ⊕ δ a (char b) = (δ a E · char a ⊕ ν? E · δ a (char a)) ⊕ ⊥

fr:mainmatter.html:p: which is an equation defining δ a E in terms of δ a E. There is no structural computation here: δ a E can only be obtained as the least fixed point of that equation. This is exactly why the classical functional-pearl implementation (Might–Darais–Spiewak 2011) needs laziness, observable sharing, and memoized fixed points — and why nullability there is also a least-fixed-point computation. Both difficulties come from a nonterminal being reachable by δ without any character being consumed first.

fr:title.text: The keystone: guardedness cuts every self-differentiation branch

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The keystone: guardedness cuts every self-differentiation branch

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A grammar is guarded when, in every production, each nonterminal occurrence is preceded by a non-nullable prefix — you cannot reach the nonterminal without first consuming at least one terminal. (E above is not guarded: its recursive E is the leading factor, preceded by nothing.)

Keystone Lemma. On the guarded fragment, δ c is a total function definable by structural recursion, computed with one unfolding of each fixed point and no auxiliary fixed point or memoization; moreover it sends guarded grammars to guarded grammars.

Why. The only way δ c fails to terminate structurally is if computing δ c X for a nonterminal X requires computing δ c X again — the cyclic equation we saw for E. That happens iff δ c can descend to a differentiated occurrence of X, i.e. iff X is reachable in the production body without passing a consuming prefix. Guardedness forbids exactly this. Consider where a guarded X sits: behind a non-nullable prefix A, as A · (⋯X⋯). The product rule splits differentiation of A · (⋯X⋯) into two branches:

html:ul.html:li: δ c A · (⋯X⋯) — keeps the X-containing tail unchanged, so X is carried along as an undifferentiated leaf; and
ν? A · δ c (⋯X⋯) — the branch that would recurse toward δ c X, but A is non-nullable, so ν? A = ⊥ and this whole branch is ⊥.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So δ c reaches every nonterminal only through the first branch, as a leaf it does not differentiate. Concretely, computing δ c X for a guarded X unfolds X's body once and makes a single structural pass, treating every nonterminal in the body (recursive or not) as an opaque leaf, because each is guarded and its ν?-gate is ⊥. The pass therefore calls δ c on no nonterminal at all — it cannot diverge, and it cannot form a cycle (even a mutual one). The output is a finite expression over the original nonterminals. ∎

The contrast with E: for E the recursive occurrence has an empty (hence nullable) prefix, so the ν? A gate is ε rather than ⊥, the second branch survives, and δ a E is forced to recurse into δ a E. The guard is precisely the syntactic condition that keeps that gate shut.

fr:title.text: Worked example: aⁿbⁿ (guarded, not regular)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let S = (char a · S · char b) ⊕ ε. The recursive S is guarded — it sits behind the non-nullable char a. First derivative:

html:p.html:code: δ a S = δ a (char a · (S · char b)) ⊕ δ a ε
= [ δ a (char a) · (S · char b) ⊕ ν?(char a) · δ a (S · char b) ] ⊕ ⊥
= [ ε · (S · char b) ⊕ ⊥ · δ a (S · char b) ] ⊕ ⊥

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notice the second branch ν?(char a) · δ a (S · char b) became ⊥ because ν?(char a) = ⊥. This is the gate closing: we never had to compute δ a (S · char b), so the computation of δ a S terminates in one unfold, and the result S · char b carries the original S undifferentiated.
Now a residual like S · char b does have S as its leading factor, so its own derivative genuinely calls δ a S:

html:p.html:code: δ a (S · char b) = δ a S · char b ⊕ ν? S · δ a (char b) = (S · char b) · char b ⊕ (ε · ⊥) = S · char b · char b

fr:mainmatter.html:p: But δ a S here is just the terminating one-unfold computation above (= S · char b), so there is no infinite regress — only a finite chain of residuals S, S · char b, S · char b · char b, …, each a finite expression over the original S. The state space is infinite (this grammar is not regular), but see below: that never matters for a single parse.

fr:title.text: Nullability collapses for the same reason

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Nullability collapses for the same reason

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For general CFGs, ν? is itself a least fixed point: whether a nonterminal is nullable can depend recursively on whether it is nullable. The guard removes this too, by the identical mechanism. A guarded recursive occurrence sits behind a non-nullable prefix, and
ν?(char a · X) = ν?(char a) · ν? X = ⊥ · ν? X = ⊥, for any X.

So a production containing a guarded recursive occurrence is non-nullable outright, regardless of the occurrence's own nullability — the recursive dependency is severed. Nullability of μX. F is then determined entirely by the non-recursive (base) alternatives of F, computable by structural recursion with no iteration to a fixed point. For aⁿbⁿ:
ν? S = ν?(char a · S · char b) ⊕ ν? ε = ⊥ ⊕ ε = ε (nullable, via the ε branch), computed without ever consulting ν? S.
This is why sss-00A5 is clean on the guarded fragment, and the same ν?-computation doubles as the check that a grammar really is guarded.

fr:title.text: What does not collapse — and why it is harmless

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What does not collapse — and why it is harmless

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Infinitely many derivatives. As the aⁿbⁿ example shows, a guarded (indeed any non-regular) grammar has infinitely many distinct derivative states, so there is no finite derivative automaton to precompute. This sounds alarming but is irrelevant to actually parsing: parsing a fixed input w takes exactly |w| derivative steps, each a total finite operation, and the parser is structurally recursive on the input list. You never enumerate the state space; you only ever walk one path of length |w| through it. (This is the same observation sss-00A6 makes as "infinite but regular-in-the-right-sense".)

Description blow-up. The product rule duplicates subgrammars — δ c (A · B) mentions B in one branch and δ c B in the other — so a naively-represented residual can grow exponentially in |w|. The remedy is compaction: algebraic simplification after each step (⊥ · x = ⊥, ε · x = x, x ⊕ ⊥ = x, and sharing of common nonterminals). The essential point for us is that compaction is an optimization, not a correctness requirement: a total, correct parser exists without it (each step is already total), so compaction and its semantics-preservation proof can be added later, purely for performance. This is the one place where the general-CFG performance story (cubic only with compaction, per Adams–Hollenbeck–Might 2016) still applies — but it is decoupled from totality and correctness.
With the keystone lemma in hand the remaining work is small and well-scoped:

html:ol.html:li: Totality and guard-preservation of δ — formalize the keystone lemma: on the guarded fragment δ c is total, structural, and maps guarded grammars to guarded grammars. This discharges the "μ is the part most likely to need care" flag of sss-00A6 and the corresponding risk; the care needed is precisely the ν?-gate argument above.

The parser as a fold / Löb fixed point — the length-recursion parser of sss-00A8, parse G (c ∷ w) = deriv⁻¹ (parse (δ c G) w), producing parse trees by reshaping along the derivative iso, optionally recast as the (Brz) Löb fixed point of sss-00EY / sss-00EX for a modality-native presentation (the guarded recursion is exactly what Löb discharges). Its output is the parse forest ⟦G⟧ w, per sss-00F0.

Soundness and completeness are automatic — the derivative commutation ⟦ δ c G ⟧ ≅ ⟦ G ⟧ ⟜ char c of sss-00A7 is a proof-relevant iso, so the fold is the bijection ⟦G⟧ w ≅ ⟦δ_w G⟧ ε; there is no separate correctness proof, and parse trees / semantic actions ride along the isos. Because δ is structural, no fixed-point / domain-theoretic reasoning is needed.
(Optional) Compaction with preservation — for performance only: prove each simplification rule is a grammar isomorphism, so parse trees / semantic actions are preserved.

fr:title.text: Precision: "guarded", not "non-left-recursive"

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The exact restriction is the ▷-guard of sss-00AC: every self-reference under a non-nullable prefix. This is strictly stronger than "not directly left-recursive". Consider hidden left recursion, A = (B · A) ⊕ c with B nullable: A is not the syntactic leading factor, but because B can vanish, A is still reachable with no character consumed, so ν? B = ε keeps the dangerous branch open and δ c A again becomes cyclic. Guardedness rules this out too — it is about consumption, not syntactic position. So state the fragment as guarded / productive.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Specialise {\mathopen {}\left (\mathrm {L\ddot ob}_\otimes \right )\mathclose {}} to single characters (A := \texttt {String}\, c, so \texttt {String}\, c \multimap B = D_c B) and sum over the alphabet, adding the nullable base case \nu B (the I \vdash B part):

fr:title.text: Open recursion for grammars: the contextual Löb rule

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Open recursion for grammars: the contextual Löb rule

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The closed Löb principle {\mathopen {}\left (\rhd A \vdash A\right )\mathclose {}} \Rightarrow {\mathopen {}\left (\top \vdash A\right )\mathclose {}} for the constructed \rhd builds a global term \top \vdash A. That is enough to define a closed recursive grammar, but not to define a recursive parser in a context — parametrised combinators, threaded accumulators, precedence-indexed families. This note records the open (contextual) form as precise entailments, and pins the exact side condition, sharpening sss-00BD's discovery that \mathsf {next} is coalgebra structure rather than a theorem.

The rule. Internalise closed Löb at the exponential \Gamma \Rightarrow A. From \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \Gamma \Rightarrow A closed Löb gives \top \vdash \Gamma \Rightarrow A, i.e. \Gamma \vdash A. Uncurrying the premise, open guarded recursion is

The recursive call is the delayed \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}}; the hypotheses in \Gamma are available now. At \Gamma = \top it collapses (\top \Rightarrow A \cong A) back to closed Löb \rhd A \vdash A. Note \And is a type former and \vdash the hom, so the premise is the single entailment above — not \Gamma conjoined with a judgement.

The catch: firing the call. To apply \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}} you must first produce \rhd \Gamma and use later-applicativity. That needs \mathsf {next}_\Gamma : \Gamma \vdash \rhd \Gamma , which by sss-00BD is not free: it is exactly an \mathsf {IsCoalgebra}\,\Gamma structure, i.e. a suffix-closed \Gamma . So the whole content of "open" reduces to one condition:

html:blockquote.html:p: Open recursion over a context \Gamma is available iff \Gamma carries \mathsf {next}_\Gamma , i.e. iff \Gamma is suffix-closed (a \rhd -coalgebra).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two sources of the step. The delayed argument the recursive call consumes can arrive two ways.

html:ul.html:li: By \mathsf {next} — when \Gamma is a coalgebra. Constant grammars \Delta S, the unit \top (the canonical \top -coalgebra of sss-00BD), and any \rhd B are suffix-closed, so \mathsf {next} exists on them.

By consumption — the parsing-specific route, needing no \mathsf {next}. If the recursive occurrence sits behind A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} with A positive (A\,\varepsilon = \varnothing : no empty parse), then {\mathopen {}\left (A \otimes X\right )\mathclose {}}\,w depends on X only at proper suffixes of w; hence A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} factors through \rhd , and \mu X.\,\mathrm {base} \oplus A \otimes X is a guarded fixed point. The \otimes pays the step that \mathsf {next} would.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This is the precise form of "guardedness by consuming a token": \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} is the single-character \rhd of sss-00AC, and A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} for positive A is its many-step generalisation.

html:ol.html:li: Kleene iteration. \mathsf {iter}\,A := \mu X.\, I \oplus A \otimes X for positive A. Open in the grammar parameter A, which is substituted and sits inside the guard — no \mathsf {next} needed. Cf. greedy Kleene star.

Left folds (\mathsf {chainl1}). Parse p\,{\mathopen {}\left (\mathit {op}\,p\right )\mathclose {}}^{\ast } threading an accumulator a : \Delta {\mathopen {}\left (\mathrm {Tree}\right )\mathclose {}}. The accumulator lives in a constant grammar — a coalgebra — so the contextual rule applies with \Gamma = \Delta {\mathopen {}\left (\mathrm {Tree}\right )\mathclose {}}.

Pratt / precedence climbing. \mathsf {pratt} : \Delta \mathbb {N} \vdash \mathrm {Parser}\,E with \mathsf {pratt}\,p recursing at a fresh level p'. This is exactly the precedence-indexed Löb family of sss-00BZ item 1, \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Pi p.\,\mathrm {Parser}\,E\right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \Pi p.\,\mathrm {Parser}\,E; the context \Delta \mathbb {N} is constant, hence a coalgebra, so \rhd distributes through the \Pi .

Attribute grammars. Inherited attributes flow into the recursive calls — the threaded context \Gamma ; synthesized attributes are the result A. The rule applies exactly when the inherited attribute is suffix-closed, which is automatic for position-independent (constant) attributes. A position-varying inherited attribute — a grammar indexed by the input already consumed — is not a coalgebra; this is precisely the boundary of genuinely context-sensitive parsing.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The dividing line. Substituted parameters, constant threads, and \rhd -guarded self-references are all coalgebras, so essentially every standard combinator is open-recursible without the applicative structure of \rhd . The one thing genuinely ruled out is transporting a position-dependent grammar down into the recursion — an inherited attribute indexed by the consumed prefix — which is where sss-00BD's missing \mathsf {next} actually bites.

Semantically this is nothing new beyond sss-00A8: the same well-founded-on-string-length induction that proves closed Löb relativises to any coalgebra context \Gamma , and that relativisation is the rule above.

fr:title.text: Open directions for parser-combinators in dependent Lambek

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Open directions for parser-combinators in dependent Lambek

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Brainstorm capturing seven open directions for the parser combinator work tracked in sss-00BY. Each subtree is a short sketch — definitions, candidate approaches, and where they'd land in the existing library. Nothing here is implemented; each item is a starting point for a follow-up.

fr:title.text: 1. Pratt grammars parametric in precedence and fixity

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: 1. Pratt grammars parametric in precedence and fixity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The generic parser in Examples.PrattRDLaterGen fixes one precedence level and right-associativity. To carry precedence p \in \{0, \dots , N\} and per-operator fixity, three viable encodings:

html:ul.html:li: Stratified inductive grammar. Index the grammar functor by precedence level: E_p := E_{p-1} \mid E_{p-1}\, op_p\, E_p (right-assoc) or with iteration for left-assoc. This is a mutually indexed inductive — define the functor F : \mathrm {Fin}\,N \to \mathrm {Functor}\,(\mathrm {Fin}\,N) and take \mu F. The parser becomes a finite tuple of mutually recursive Löb-fixed parsers, one per level.

Single grammar, precedence-indexed parser. Keep the grammar flat (E := A \mid A\, \mathrm {Op}\, E) and let the parser enforce precedence at parse time. Parser type: \mathrm {Lev} \to \mathsf {string} \vdash \mathsf {Parser}\,E. Löb-fix the whole family: \triangleright (\forall p.\,\mathsf {Parser}\,E) \vdash \forall p.\,\mathsf {Parser}\,E. This needs \triangleright to distribute through \Pi , which is standard in guarded type theory and should hold for the left-handed later modality in use here.

Per-operator threshold. Each operator carries (lbp, rbp). The parser checks \mathit {lbp}(\mathit {op}) > \mathrm {minPrec} and recurses with \mathit {rbp}(\mathit {op}). Right-assoc: \mathit {rbp} = \mathit {lbp} - 1; left-assoc: \mathit {rbp} = \mathit {lbp}. The left-assoc case requires the "loop" rather than "fold" recursion shape — see item 6 for the substring-modality angle.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Spec extension:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
record OpInfo : Type where field prec : ℕ rightAssoc : Bool
record PrattSpec : Type₁ where field AI : Type ℓ-zero ; isSetAI : isSet AI OI : Type ℓ-zero ; isSetOI : isSet OI opInfo : OI → OpInfo
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The hard part isn't the spec — it's the parser body. The Löb-fixed precedence-indexed family is probably the cleanest path; the stratified inductive view is the cleanest grammar-level description.

fr:title.text: 2. Performance for witness-level parse-tree tests

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The current tests assert acceptP w ≡ true via Bool-valued acceptance because building the full parse witness blows up term size. Sources of the blowup:

html:ul.html:li: Splittings: every \otimes carries a (w_1, w_2, p : w \equiv w_1 ++ w_2) record. Compositions stack these records.
Inductive grammar \mu F uses liftG/lowerG wrappers that don't reduce away under DSL combinators.
The Maybe⊗r, fmap, ⊕-elim chains produce nested case analyses that normalise to large terms even on small inputs.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Candidate fixes, roughly cheapest first:

html:ul.html:li: Bool-valued acceptance is sufficient most of the time. The current trick.

Structural test predicate. Define matchTree : Expr → BoolTree (a flat ADT mirroring the parse shape), recurse on the recognized witness, and compare against an expected BoolTree. This sidesteps splittings entirely. The "compare" reduces to Bool equality on a tree of tags.

Rewrite rules for monoidal laws. Declare \otimes -unit, \otimes -assoc, and \otimes -symmetry-equations as BUILTIN REWRITE, so that the elaborator collapses chains of ⊗-assoc⁻ ∘g ⊗-assoc during normalisation. Cubical paths complicate this — would need either eq-style rewrites (cf. AsEquality port) or careful `--rewriting` discipline.

Specialised evaluator. Write \mathsf {eval} : (\mathsf {string} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\,(A \otimes \mathsf {string})) \to \mathrm {List}\,\mathrm {Sym} \to \mathrm {Maybe}\,(\mathrm {AST}\,A \times \mathrm {List}\,\mathrm {Sym}) that interprets each DSL combinator on flat data structures (no splittings, no LiftG). Prove a correctness theorem once; then tests use eval for speed.

Two-tier opaque/transparent layers. The current eval-parser unfolds everything; consider a finer-grained eval-parser-tree marker that unfolds only the structural spine. The cubical paths in splittings would stay sealed.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The structural test predicate is probably the highest leverage — it captures the parse shape (which is what tests want to assert) without ever materialising splittings.

fr:title.text: 3. Lexing inside or outside LambekD

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two questions: can we do lexing in the DSL, and what's the ergonomic way to write test inputs.

In-DSL lexing. A lexer is a parser whose target grammar is a token stream. Building one in the DSL is mechanically possible: Kleene-*, \oplus , and disjunction are available. A LexerSpec record would carry per-token regexes plus a priority order (for longest-match / first-match disambiguation). Output: \mathsf {string}_\mathrm {raw} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\,(\mathrm {TokenList} \otimes \varepsilon ). The cost is non-trivial — whitespace handling, keyword tables, longest-match, error recovery — and offers no real benefit over an ordinary Agda function unless we want to reason semantically about lexer correctness in the same vocabulary as the parser.
Ergonomic test inputs. The pragmatic answer is to keep lexing external: an Agda function
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: lex : Agda.Builtin.String.String → List Sym lex s = lex' (primStringToList s) where lex' : List Char → List Sym lex' [] = [] lex' ('a' ∷ cs) = ⌜a⌝ ∷ lex' cs lex' ('+' ∷ cs) = ⌜+⌝ ∷ lex' cs ...
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then acceptExpr (lex "a+b*a") typechecks and reduces identically to the hand-written a ∷ +t ∷ b ∷ *t ∷ a ∷ []. For multi-character tokens (let, =, identifiers), the lexer needs maximal-munch and a keyword table — also routine in plain Agda.

For the further-out goal of writing \texttt {"let x = 5 in x"} directly: combine the lexer above with a preprocessor that recognises identifiers and literals as token-with- payload. The token type extends from a plain enum to a tagged sum: Token = LET ∣ IN ∣ EQ ∣ IDENT String ∣ INT ℕ, and the parser's alphabet becomes this richer type (with appropriate isSet proof, e.g. via a retract through \mathbb {N} \uplus \mathrm {String} \uplus \mathrm {Fin}\,k).

Semantic bridging. If desired, prove \mathsf {lex}^* \equiv \mathsf {lex}_\mathrm {DSL} as a refinement theorem connecting the external lexer to an in-DSL specification. This pays for itself if you want end-to-end soundness statements ("parse of "a+b" produces this AST"), but isn't needed for the test-ergonomics use case alone.

fr:title.text: 4. Type-level guarantee of parser completeness

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The current type \mathsf {Parser}\,A = \mathsf {Maybe}\,(A \otimes \mathsf {string}) doesn't promise that nothing only fires on strings outside the language. A few ways to fix this in the type signature:

html:ul.html:li: Decision-procedure parsers. Replace the type with \mathsf {Parser}_!\,A = \mathsf {string} \cong (A \otimes \mathsf {string}) \oplus \mathrm {NoParse}_A where the right summand captures negative information ("no prefix of the input is in A"). NoParse is the tricky bit — it might be definable as \mathsf {string} \multimap (A \to \bot ) or via decidability witnesses.
Refinement-typed parsers. Bundle the morphism with its soundness/completeness proofs:
html:ul.html:pre: record CompleteParser (A : Grammar ℓ) : Type where field parse : string ⊢ Maybe (A ⊗ string) sound : ∀ w → parse w ≡ inl r → ⟨A w⟩ on (r.fst.fst) complete : ∀ w → parse w ≡ inr _ → ¬ ∃ accepting-split-of w
html:ul.html:li: Unambiguous-grammar route. For unambiguous LL(k) grammars, derive the parser directly from a grammar-equivalence proof \mathsf {string} \cong A \oplus \neg A. The Examples.BinOp.LL⟨1⟩ family already has this structure for LL(1); generalising the technique would be the principled route.
Total-by-construction. Index parsers by their language denotation; require that combinators preserve a "completeness" predicate (cf. item 5).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The cheapest practical move is the refinement-typed bundle — add soundness and completeness as ancillary fields that parser combinators thread through automatically. The unambiguous-grammar route is the most principled but requires a much heavier metatheory investment.

fr:title.text: 5. Danielsson's total parser combinators

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Danielsson's Total Parser Combinators (ICFP'10) builds total parsers in Agda by:

html:ol.html:li: Indexing parsers by the language they recognise (\mathsf {Parser}\,A\,L produces values of type A from inputs in L).
Encoding "consumes at least one token" as a type-level annotation (\mathit {null} vs \mathit {nonNull}) so that the combinator algebra rejects unproductive recursion.
Using coinductive/depth-indexed types so that the parser is total by construction.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Mapping to dependent Lambek:

html:ul.html:li: Language indexing is automatic — the grammar A is the language denotation, baked into the parser type.

Consumption annotation maps to the later modality: ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ requires a non-empty static prefix, which is exactly Danielsson's "must consume". So \triangleright on the left-handed modality corresponds to Danielsson's "delayed parser, productive after consumption".

Productivity / totality maps to Löb induction: the fixed-point combinator lob is well-defined precisely because every recursive call passes through \triangleright , mirroring how Danielsson's coinductive parsers are productive because every corecursive call passes through the depth annotation.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So yes, the techniques apply, and the correspondence is reasonably tight: \triangleright \leftrightarrow consumption annotation, lob \leftrightarrow guarded fixed point, fixP \leftrightarrow fix on coinductive parsers. Direct adaptations worth importing:

html:ul.html:li: The "null"/"nonNull" distinction would let us forbid fixP id-style nonsense at the type level.

Danielsson's algebraic laws ((p₁ ⊕ p₂) ⊕ p₃ ≡ p₁ ⊕ (p₂ ⊕ p₃), left/right unit, etc.) transfer to our combinators essentially verbatim, and proving them would let combinator-level rewriting drive test-time normalisation (cf. item 2).

fr:title.text: 6. Substring-modality later \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Current modalities: \triangleright (left-handed, consumes a non-empty prefix) and \triangleright ^r (right-handed, consumes a non-empty suffix). A natural third option is the substring modality \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}, expressing "later on any proper substring". sss-00B9 already sketches one shape for this; below fleshes out the elimination rule and the use case.
Semantic definition (on grammars):

i.e. there exists a decomposition w = u_1 \cdot w' \cdot u_2 with at least one of u_1, u_2 non-empty, and A holds on w'. (The two summands handle "left margin non-empty" and "right margin non-empty"; their overlap is also non-empty on both sides, which is fine since \oplus of A-witnesses is just "either witness".)
Elimination rule, by analogy with ▷-app-NE:

Fixed-point principle: \mathsf {lob}_\mathrm {sub} : (\triangleright _\mathrm {sub}\, A \vdash A) \to (\top \vdash A). Well-foundedness comes from |w'| < |w| whenever w = u_1 \cdot w' \cdot u_2 and one of u_1, u_2 is non-empty.

html:ul.html:li: Bracketed-content recursion without staging. Currently the parens parser consumes \langle , recurses on the suffix, then checks the inner leftover for \rangle . With \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}, we could directly recurse on "the content between \langle and \rangle " once we've found the matching close — a much more natural decomposition.

Dyck and similar grammars. The inner D in \langle D \rangle D is a proper substring of the outer input, not a suffix. With \triangleright _\mathrm {sub} we'd express this directly rather than via the suffix-and-leftover dance. See item 7.

Left-associative iteration. Reframe a left-assoc operator loop as: parse an atom a_n at the end of the input, recurse on the substring "everything before a_n" to get a_1 \, \mathit {op} \, \cdots \, \mathit {op} \, a_{n-1}. The recursive call is on a proper substring.
Two-sided patterns like a^n\, b\, c^n. The marker b is in the middle; recursion on the substring strictly between the two "ends" is the natural shape.

fr:title.text: 7. Dyck as a guarded fixed point

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: 7. Dyck as a guarded fixed point

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cass's intuition (per discussion): the Dyck grammar can be described not just as the initial algebra \mu (I \oplus \langle \, X\, \rangle \, X) but as a guarded fixed point of a functor that turns "later grammars" into "current grammars" by consuming brackets.
Concretely:
The question marks are exactly the elimination of \triangleright _?: each occurrence of X is consumed at a position where the input has already given up at least one character. Two Xs appear:

html:ul.html:li: The inner X matches the contents between \langle and \rangle . Its input is a proper substring of the parent input (margins \langle and \rangle ++ \cdots on either side, both non-empty). Naturally a use of \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}.
The outer X matches the suffix after the closing \rangle . Its input is a proper suffix of the parent input. A use of \triangleright (left-handed).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So the modality at the recursive position is a sort of join: either \triangleright or \triangleright _\mathrm {sub} suffices to witness productivity. One could take \triangleright _\mathrm {join} as the disjunction (a third modality), or use a heterogeneous functor where each X position is annotated with its own modality.

Connection to well-foundedness. The \mu -view of Dyck is the initial algebra of a polynomial functor; well-foundedness comes from structural induction on the inductive type. The guarded view gives an alternative justification: the unique fixed point under productivity. Both views coincide because Dyck is unambiguous — every Dyck word has exactly one parse tree.
Guarded fixed-point operator on grammars. The required primitive is

such that \mathsf {gfix}\, F \cong F(\mathrm {next}(\mathsf {gfix}\,F)) as grammars. This is the grammar-level analogue of lob (which operates at the term level on parser combinators). With it, Dyck = gfix DyckF, and we'd have a clean equivalence Dyck ≅ μ DyckBaseFunctor to relate the two encodings.

Payoff. Importing guarded-type-theory technology (clock variables, ticks, Iris-style modal reasoning) to grammars. Useful for: equivalences between \mu and \mathsf {gfix} definitions; modular productivity proofs that compose; semantic accounts of non-well-founded grammar definitions (e.g. infinite-arity \oplus _d where the index set itself is given by a guarded process).

fr:title.text: State and Attempt Löb Induction for ▷

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: State and Attempt Löb Induction for ▷

fr:mainmatter.html:p: State and attempt the Löb induction principle lob : (▷ A ⊢ A) → (⊤ ⊢ A) for the candidate ▷ of sss-00B9. This is the test of the whole approach: if Löb holds, the modality is genuinely "later"; if it fails, examine why before fixing the definition.

Sketch to follow. From ▷ A ⊢ A and next (sss-00BD) build \rhd A \vdash \rhd A as a \sqrt [w]{}-coalgebra in each component; uniqueness on each component forces the global fixed point, and the limit of "the unique fixed point" is the unique fixed point of the limit.

Compare against sss-00A8. The character-by- character flavour of the proof matches the well-founded-on-string-length recursion already used to build the Brzozowski parser. If the proof goes through, check whether it reuses that recursion verbatim — that would be evidence Löb here is the same principle, repackaged as a type former.

html:ul.html:li: The "uniqueness on each component" step might require a global productivity assumption that doesn't follow from ▷ A ⊢ A alone.
The empty-string boundary may sneak back in via the limit, even though we excluded it from the indexing.
Composing two limits (the indexed product and the recursive fixed point) may need a Fubini-style commutation that is genuinely nontrivial.

fr:title.text: Later Operator ▶ as Internalised Guard

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The plan is self-contained without any modalities: productivity is a side condition on CFGDesc, nullability is an external decision sss-00A5, and well-foundedness is operational recursion on length sss-00A8. A later operator ▶ would internalise each of these into the type system, making the same construction fall out of guarded fixpoint rather than a sequence of external theorems.
Two natural slots for ▶:

html:p.html:strong: 1. As the guard on μ in CFGDesc.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The current productivity condition on CFGDesc ("every self-reference sits under a non-nullable prefix") is a bespoke later modality indexed by "must consume ≥1 char." First-class ▶ replaces the side condition with a syntactic requirement:

where F is any unconstrained CFGDesc-style functor. This is exactly the trade-up that the Grammar.SequentialUnambiguity.Nullable scaffolding already gestures at: ¬Nullable A is a proposition about a grammar; ▶ would be a grammar constructor.

The paper's guard functor (F ↓₀) X i = F (λ j → (j ≺ i) × X j) i is already a parameterised later modality: the parameter is the well-founded relation ≺, not a global clock. So the machinery in IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs.lagda is morally a per-index ▶, and moving to a syntactic ▶ is just factoring that indexing into the type theory.

html:p.html:strong: 2. As the meaning of A ⟜ char c.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Recall from ⟜-as-derivative that
(A ⟜ char c) w = A (c ∷ w),

i.e. inhabiting A ⟜ char c requires being fed one character before producing an A. This is the defining behaviour of a later modality: availability delayed by one step, where "step" = "one character consumed."
Under this reading the Brzozowski identity char c · A ≅ δ c A becomes an applicativity law:
char c · (A ⟜ char c) ⊢ A (▶-apply)
and the derivative-based parser is a guarded fixpoint:

html:p.html:code: parse : μ self. (char? ⟜ ε ⊕ (Σ c. ▶ (parse (δ c G))))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: where the self-reference is guarded by ▶ ≡ (_ ⟜ char c), and the well-foundedness witness F-ε⁻¹ of c2a-morph is exactly the "take a later and cash it in" rule.

html:ul.html:li: Nullability becomes decidable by typing. ε ⊢ A iff A is ▶-free at the outer layer; no external decision needed.
Length-well-foundedness becomes automatic. Each ▶-unfold consumes exactly one character, so recursion depth ≤ input length by construction. sss-00A8's use of <-wellFounded disappears.

c2a-morph becomes guarded fixpoint. The paper's uniqueness theorem specialises to the Löb-style uniqueness of guarded fixpoints in the appropriate topos. Computational content is the same; meta-theory is cleaner.
Not on the critical path. The plan works without ▶; this tree is about a cleaner re-foundation, not a missing step.

Integration cost. Adding ▶ as a primitive means revisiting every grammar operation (tensor, residual, fixed points) to specify its interaction with ▶. Feasible, but a larger design commitment than "a few side conditions."

Which ▶? Classical guarded type theory's ▶ is character-agnostic (one "tick" per step). Ours is character-indexed (▶_c A = A ⟜ char c). The paper's (F ↓₀) sits in between — indexed by an abstract ≺. Whether to use a single ▶ or a character-indexed family is itself a design question.

html:ol.html:li: Prototype ▶ A as an alias for Σ c : Alphabet. A ⟜ char c (character-indexed form) inside the existing calculus, without new primitives.
Re-state nullability as a syntactic check on ▶-absence at the top of a description.
Re-derive c2a-morph for the single-step case and see whether the ▶-elimination rule does the work currently done by F-ε⁻¹.
Only then consider adding ▶ to CFGDesc as a primitive constructor (step 1 of sss-00A4).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open: does a character-indexed ▶ compose into a single modality after applying the "erase the character" projection? That would bridge the specific (Brzozowski-style) and generic (Löb-style) readings.

fr:title.text: Parser as Unique c2a-Morphism of a Recursive Coalgebra

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parser as Unique c2a-Morphism of a Recursive Coalgebra

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Goal: reinterpret the length-recursive parser as the unique coalgebra-to-algebra morphism produced by the c2a-morph construction of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] (file IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs.lagda, module c2a.c2a-morph).
Concretely we need to supply five pieces:

html:ol.html:li: A carrier C : ℕ → Type (indexed by input length). The coalgebra input at length n is the set of strings of that length paired with the current derivative state G.
A well-founded relation on ℕ: the standard _<_, with well-foundedness from Cubical.Induction.WellFounded.
A base endofunctor F on ℕ → Type expressing one character of progress: F X n = nullability-answer-at-0 ⊕ (Alphabet × X (n-1)).
The well-foundedness witness F-ε⁻¹ : F X n ⊢ (F ↓₀) X n coming from the fact that every recursive occurrence sits under a strictly-decreasing length.
A coalgebra c : C ⇒ F C (one step of derivative) and an algebra a : F Answer ⇒ Answer, where Answer G w = Parser ⟦ G ⟧cfg (¬ ⟦ G ⟧cfg) w.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Applying c2a.c2a-morph to these yields a morphism parse : C ⇒ Answer together with the uniqueness property inherited from the recursive-coalgebra framework. Uniqueness is exactly the statement that "the parser is the correct parser" — there is only one coalgebra-to-algebra morphism, so any alternative definition agrees with ours on every input.
Contrast with the intrinsically-recursive GCD and CYK:

html:ul.html:li: GCD is well-founded on proj₂ of ℕ × ℕ. Ours is well-founded on length of the string — the same idea (project down to ℕ, use <).

CYK uses List⁺ to sidestep nullability entirely. We cannot do that — nullability is a first-class question for CFGs — but we handle it by threading the nullability decision through the algebra at length 0.
Both GCD and CYK pay the price of defining the base functor and its well-foundedness lemma by hand. Ours pays the same price uniformly, parameterised over G : CFGDesc.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open: does c2a-morph give us extensional uniqueness (the thing we want, since grammars are propositions at each string), or does it give a stronger computational equality? IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs proves unique.unique at the indexed-set level; check whether its use of Set-level equalities causes friction with our Type-valued grammars. Tracked in risks.
